input_contract.description: A single integer n between 1 and 10000. Overflow-sensitive: the count exceeds the modulus from about n = 23 onward.

mutants.description: returns the count for a single side, not squared
treats the two sides as one row of 2n plots
returns the exact count without reducing
iterates n times instead of n-1
EQUIVALENT: no intermediate reduction, one modulo at the end
mutants.equivalence_argument: Modular reduction is a ring homomorphism: (x + y) mod m = ((x mod m) + (y mod m)) mod m, and the same for multiplication. Reducing at every step and reducing once at the end therefore give the same residue. Python integers are arbitrary precision, so the unreduced intermediate cannot overflow and the only cost is speed. Equal on every n in the specification's range.

t1-adjacency-across-the-street.why_wrong: The specification says the adjacency restriction applies only within a side and that a house places no restriction on the plot opposite it. Modelling the street as a single row imposes a constraint that does not exist.

t1-loop-runs-n-times.why_wrong: Classic off-by-one when the base case already covers the first plot. Shifts every answer one step along the recurrence.

t1-no-modulo-reduction.why_wrong: The specification says the result is reduced modulo 1000000007 rather than reported exactly. In Python nothing overflows, so this is invisible until n is large enough for the square to exceed the modulus — around n = 23.

t1-one-side-only.why_wrong: The specification's load-bearing sentence is that the total is the count for one side multiplied by itself. Solving one side and forgetting the street has two is the central trap of this problem.

t1-plain-fibonacci-base.why_wrong: Recognising the Fibonacci shape but not re-deriving the base case. With n = 1 there are two arrangements per side, not one — the empty plot counts.
